dimensions.summary: The rebuilt SDF matrix pipeline is substantially stronger than what the July audit saw. The composition machinery (shared/matrix.py + compose_prompts.py) genuinely delivers its "composition by construction" promise: largest-remainder deck sampling gives exact per-axis marginals, weights are validated all-or-nothing with a sum check, reserved slots are rejected in variables.txt, and an unusually good contract-test suite pins the real templates to the real variables file (plan-axis coverage, no orphan axes, species-pool coverage, locale mapping, seed determinism). The rewritten layers 3/4 and the new plan stage fixed the old truncation blind spot — stop_reason is checked fail-closed (only end_turn accepted), failed/truncated/malformed work is never checkpointed, poison calls are isolated per item, and an all-pending-failed SystemExit guard catches systemic outages; layer12 has exemplary test coverage of these paths. The residual risk clusters in two places. First, layer 5 is the odd stage out: it alone never inspects stop_reason (routing retryable truncations/refusals into the checkpointed 5/5/5 sentinel, i.e. a permanent silent drop under the default threshold of 7) and it trusts judge-emitted score fields without type/shape validation, where a string score wedges the run at the gate after checkpointing and missing keys silently zero-score a paid rewrite. Second, the shared done-detection idiom (existing-record AND checkpoint conjunction, identical in all four stage files) plus the unvalidated reuse of a possibly-partial prompts.jsonl means certain inconsistent-but-reachable states (torn writes, manual cleanup, hard crash) degrade to silently missing documents rather than retries or loud errors — and no stage or orchestrator ever reconciles final corpus count against the planned n_prompts, so nothing downstream would notice. Test coverage of the failure branches is complete for layer12 but thins out for layers 3-5 (layer4's exception/truncation/SystemExit paths are entirely untested — the 83% coverage gap). All fixes are small; none require design changes.

findings.title: Checkpointed id with missing jsonl record is silently dropped in all four stages
findings.evidence: pending = [d for d in drafts if d["doc_id"] not in existing and not checkpoint.is_done(d["doc_id"])] (layer4_rewrite.py:38-41). An id that is in the checkpoint but absent from rewrites.jsonl joins neither `results` (built only from `existing`) nor `pending`, so it is never retried and never reaches downstream layers — no warning is printed. Since mark_done always runs AFTER append_jsonl in every stage, a checkpointed id should always have a record; the conjunction can only ever convert 'retry' into 'silently skip'. The identical idiom appears in all four stage files.
findings.failure_scenario: A run crashes hard (power loss / kill -9) so the buffered rewrites.jsonl append is lost while the separately-written _checkpoint.json survives — or an operator deletes a torn/bad line from a stage jsonl during recovery from the known load_jsonl partial-line crash but leaves the checkpoint. On --resume the document vanishes from the run: not rescored, not redrafted, absent from the final corpus, with no message. Nothing reconciles corpus size against sdf.n_prompts, so a delivered corpus is silently short.
findings.recommendation: Drop `and not checkpoint.is_done(...)` from the pending filter in all four stages (record presence in the stage jsonl is the true done signal; the checkpoint adds nothing because mark_done follows append_jsonl) — or keep it but detect the inconsistent state explicitly: `orphans = [id for id in checkpoint ids if id not in existing]` and either warn loudly and re-queue them or abort. Additionally have run.py print a per-layer reconciliation line (planned N, planned-ok M, drafted K, rewritten J, scored I, corpus H) so silent drops become visible.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified the pending-filter conjunction at all four cited locations (layer12_plan.py:54-57, layer3_draft.py:39-42, layer4_rewrite.py:38-41, layer5_score.py:43-46): an id in _checkpoint.json but missing from the stage jsonl joins neither results (built solely from the jsonl) nor pending, with no warning. append_jsonl precedes mark_done in every stage, so the is_done clause can only convert retry into silent skip. Both scenario paths hold: neither append_jsonl nor Checkpoint.mark_done fsyncs (shared/utils.py:48-52, 445-453), so power loss can persist the checkpoint while losing the jsonl append; and load_jsonl (utils.py:55-65) has no per-line error handling, so an operator deleting a torn line while leaving the checkpoint reproduces the drop. sdf_pipeline/run.py contains no corpus-size reconciliation against sdf.n_prompts.

findings.title: Layer 5 never checks stop_reason: truncation/refusal becomes a checkpointed 5/5/5 permanent drop
findings.evidence: score_one calls api.call_claude without return_stop_reason=True (layer5_score.py:56-63); a max_tokens-truncated or refused response (empty/partial text) hits extract_json_object, raises JSONDecodeError, and falls into the {5,5,5, "Parse error."} record (lines 71-74) which is appended and checkpoint.mark_done'd (lines 94-95). Layers 12/3/4 all request stop_reason and skip-without-checkpoint on stop != "end_turn" (e.g. layer3_draft.py:84-86); api.py's own docstring says callers feeding training records "should also reject on stop_reason via return_stop_reason" (shared/api.py:727-729).
findings.failure_scenario: The judge model's refusal classifier fires on one document (the claude_code backend surfaces this as stop_reason='refusal' with empty text — the exact pattern seen live on DAD scope calls), or a verbose judge reply hits the 4000-token config cap mid-notes. The doc is scored 5/5/5, checkpointed, and — with the default min_score_threshold of 7 — permanently gated out of the corpus. The paid draft + rewrite is silently discarded and --resume will never re-score it, even though a retry (the remedy every sibling stage uses for exactly this failure class) would very likely succeed.
findings.recommendation: Pass return_stop_reason=True in score_one and, mirroring layers 3/4, `if stop != "end_turn": print(retry message); return None`-style skip without checkpointing (count it separately from failed_calls or include it — either way don't checkpoint). This confines the tracked 5/5/5 sentinel to genuine parse failures on complete responses, which is the only case its "re-running would re-bill without new information" rationale actually holds for.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified every claim: layer5_score.py:56-63 omits return_stop_reason; strict extract_json_object raises JSONDecodeError on empty/truncated text, hitting the 5/5/5 "Parse error." fallback (lines 71-74) which is appended and checkpointed (lines 94-95) and never re-scored on resume (lines 41-46); with min_score_threshold=7 (config.yaml:33) and max_tokens=4000 (config.yaml:19) the doc is permanently gated out (lines 105-108). Layers 12/3/4 all request stop_reason and skip-without-checkpoint (layer3_draft.py:84-86 etc.), and shared/api.py:726-729 contains the quoted guidance (as an inline comment, not a docstring — trivial mislabel). The module docstring documents the checkpoint-on-parse-error tradeoff as deliberate, but its premise (retry adds no information) does not hold for truncation/refusal, so the finding's scenario stands.

findings.title: Layer 5 judge scores are unvalidated: a non-numeric score wedges the run at the gate after checkpointing; missing keys silently zero-score
findings.evidence: scores.get("alignment", 0) etc. (layer5_score.py:79-82) store whatever JSON type the judge emitted, and the gate compares it raw: r["scores"]["alignment"] >= threshold (line 107). A string score ("alignment": "8") raises TypeError ('>=' not supported between str and int) — but only AFTER the record was appended to scores.jsonl and checkpointed (lines 94-95). On --resume the bad record is reloaded into `results` from `existing` (line 42) and the gate crashes again: the run is permanently wedged until someone hand-edits scores.jsonl. Separately, a parseable object missing the score keys (e.g. the judge nesting them under {"scores": {...}}) defaults to 0/0/0 — below any threshold — and is checkpointed without the "Parse error." flag the sentinel path gets.
findings.failure_scenario: The judge runs at the pipeline-global temperature 1.0 over thousands of documents; one reply emits "8" as a string or wraps the three integers in a nested object. String case: every subsequent run and resume of layer 5 dies with TypeError at the gate — a full-scale run that already paid for all its scoring cannot finish. Nested/missing-key case: a good document is recorded 0/0/0, permanently gated out, and looks like a legitimate quality failure in the score report rather than a judge slip.
findings.recommendation: Validate the three scores at parse time: `try: a = int(scores["alignment"]) ... except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):` and route the failure into the existing parse-error sentinel (so it is at least flagged "Parse error." for manual review) or, better, into the un-checkpointed retry path. Add tests: a string-valued score, and an object missing the keys, must not wedge the gate or silently zero-score. Also range-check 1-10 while there.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified every cited line in sdf_pipeline/layer5_score.py at current HEAD: lines 79-82 store judge values unvalidated (extract_json_object in shared/utils.py checks only dict shape, not keys/types), line 107 compares raw against int threshold 7 so a string score raises TypeError only after lines 94-95 already appended and checkpointed the record, and line 42 reloads the poisoned record from scores.jsonl on every --resume, re-crashing the gate — the wedge is real and permanent without hand-editing. The missing-key case also holds: a parseable object lacking the score keys defaults to 0/0/0 with empty notes (no "Parse error." sentinel, which fires only on JSONDecodeError) and is silently gated out. The judge runs at the global temperature 1.0 (no per-call override at lines 56-63), making the failure scenario plausible at scale.

findings.title: Partial or empty prompts.jsonl is reused on resume with no count check, silently shrinking the run
findings.evidence: if prompts_path.exists(): prompts = utils.load_jsonl(prompts_path) (layer12_plan.py:35-37) — existence alone is treated as completeness; len(prompts) is never compared to sdf["n_prompts"]. The file is written record-by-record in a plain append loop (lines 48-49) after the full list is composed, so a disk-full IOError, kill, or crash inside that loop leaves a well-formed but short file that every later --resume silently accepts as the whole plan.
findings.failure_scenario: A 5000-prompt full-scale run dies partway through the prompts.jsonl write loop (disk full is the realistic trigger — the exception propagates, the partial file stays). The operator fixes the disk and runs --resume: the stage prints "Reusing 3200 composed prompts", plans/drafts/scores only those, and the run completes 'successfully' with a 3200-document corpus. Beyond the missing 1800 documents, the exact-marginals guarantee is gone — a prefix of the shuffled decks no longer matches the variables.txt weights exactly — and nothing downstream ever checks the count.
findings.recommendation: After reloading, verify `len(prompts) == sdf["n_prompts"]` and abort with a clear message on mismatch (composition is seeded and reads the run's frozen snapshot, so deleting the file and recomposing is safe and reproducible — say so in the error). Alternatively write prompts to a temp file and os.replace() into place so prompts.jsonl existing implies it is complete.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified sdf_pipeline/layer12_plan.py:35-37 (existence check, load, "Reusing N" print — no len(prompts) vs sdf["n_prompts"] comparison anywhere) and lines 48-49 (per-record append_jsonl loop after the full list is composed). load_jsonl (shared/utils.py:55-65) accepts any well-formed short file, resume plans only the loaded prompt_ids, and deck_sample (shared/matrix.py:137-150) guarantees exact per-variable marginals only over the full n — a prefix breaks that guarantee. Minor nuance: a disk-full failure can leave a torn last line that makes resume crash loudly with JSONDecodeError instead of silently shrinking, but a kill/crash between appends (or disk-full at a record boundary) produces exactly the silent scenario claimed.

findings.title: Failure-path tests missing for layers 3-5: layer4's exception/truncation/SystemExit branches are entirely untested
findings.evidence: Coverage report: layer4_rewrite.py 83% missing 62-66 (the per-item exception handler), 73-75 (raw is None retry path), 77-78 (truncation retry path), 97 (all-failed SystemExit); layer3_draft.py missing 85-86 (truncation branch); layer5_score.py missing 64-68 (API-exception skip), 91-92 (failed_calls counting), 99 (SystemExit). test_sdf_layers.py confirms: TestLayer4Rewrite (line 246) has no poison-call, truncation, or systemic-failure test, TestLayer5Score none either — only TestLayer12Plan covers all three. CLAUDE.md's testing rules require a malformed-response fallback and money-path coverage for every stage.
findings.failure_scenario: The poison-call isolation and truncation-retry logic in layer 4 — the alignment-critical, most expensive stage — is exactly the code that protects paid work when a $50+ run hits a usage-policy false positive or a max_tokens truncation. It is currently unexecuted by CI: a future edit that breaks the `raw is None` tuple contract, checkpoints truncated rewrites, or inverts the SystemExit condition merges green and is only discovered mid-paid-run.
findings.recommendation: Port layer12's three tests (test_one_poison_call_does_not_kill_the_layer, test_truncated_*_retried_on_resume, test_all_*_calls_failing_is_a_systemic_error) to TestLayer3Draft (truncation only — the other two exist), TestLayer4Rewrite (all three), and TestLayer5Score (poison-skip + systemic). The dispatcher-stub pattern is already in the file; this is an afternoon of copy-adapt.
findings.verifier_notes: Read sdf_pipeline/layer4_rewrite.py, layer5_score.py, layer3_draft.py and tests/test_sdf_layers.py at current main: layer4's exception handler (62-66), raw-is-None retry (72-75), truncation branch (76-78), and SystemExit (96-100) exist and no test in TestLayer4Rewrite (line 246) exercises any of them (no raising stub, no non-end_turn tuple, no pytest.raises); same for layer5's exception skip (64-68), failed_calls (90-92), SystemExit (98-102); layer3 misses only the truncation branch (84-86) as claimed, having poison/systemic tests at lines 212/235. TestLayer12Plan is indeed the only class covering all three failure modes, and the e2e smoke test is happy-path only. Exact coverage percentages could not be re-run (coverage/pytest-cov not installed; read-only), but branch-by-branch inspection matches every claimed missing range within one line. Minor nit: layer4 does have a malformed-response (missing-tags) test, so only the exception/truncation/SystemExit gap — the finding's core claim — stands, and it stands fully.

findings.title: A downstream-only axis with zero values silently empties the entire deck sample
findings.evidence: deck_sample builds one deck per axis and returns [dict(zip(axes, row)) for row in zip(*decks)] (matrix.py:151); an axis with no values yields an empty deck and the unstrict zip truncates every other deck to zero rows — verified live: deck_sample({"a": ["x","y"], "b": []}, ..., n=10) returns 0 assignments with no error. compose_records' missing-values guard (compose_prompts.py:286-291) checks only plan_axes; downstream-only axes (explicitly supported — variables consumed by layer3.txt but not layers1-2.txt) are appended unchecked at line 299.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor adds a new layer3-only axis to variables.txt, then comments out all its values while iterating on the list (the file encourages comment dividers). Every real axis today is a plan axis so nothing currently trips this, but the moment such an axis exists the whole run composes zero prompts — the pipeline prints "deck-sampled 0 prompts" / "Composed 0 prompts" and finishes cleanly with an empty corpus rather than raising, and the orphan-axis contract test does not catch emptiness (the axis is still 'consumed').
findings.recommendation: In compose_records, extend the missing-values check to every sampled axis, not just plan_axes: `missing = [n for n in axes if not values.get(n)]`. Belt-and-braces: pass strict=True to both zips in deck_sample so a length mismatch can never truncate silently, and add a parse-level error (or the same check in split_weights) for a header with zero values.

findings.title: is_incoherent fails open on malformed plans: INCOHERENT in the working notes converts a retryable failure into a checkpointed rejection
findings.evidence: When a plan has no <document_description> tags, is_incoherent falls back to a bare word-scan of the first 2000 characters (compose_prompts.py:236-239: `return bool(INCOHERENT_RE.search(plan[:2000]))`) — a window that contains the <document_planning> working notes. In layer12_plan.py:89-91, description-None + incoherent-True is checkpointed as a deliberate rejection instead of taking the retry path, and layer3 drops it (layer3_draft.py:36).
findings.failure_scenario: The template itself instructs the model about the INCOHERENT convention, so planning notes plausibly discuss it ("checking whether this combination is INCOHERENT — no, a podcast about pest control works..."). If that same response then mangles or omits the description tags — the exact malformed case the fail-closed design is meant to retry — the word-scan flags it incoherent, layer12 checkpoints it as a deliberate rejection, and the combination is silently and permanently dropped from the corpus instead of being retried on resume.
findings.recommendation: Scope the fallback word-scan to tag-less LEGACY plans only, and make it stricter for current output: treat INCOHERENT as deliberate only when it appears inside <document_description> tags (the template mandates it there); a tag-less response should always take the retry path regardless of vocabulary. One-line change in is_incoherent plus a test with INCOHERENT in the planning notes and no description tags.

findings.title: Layer 12 plan calls don't cache the shared system prompt though every sibling stage does
findings.evidence: layer12_plan.py:61-68 calls api.call_claude without cache_system=True, while layers 3, 4, and 5 all pass cache_system=True for their identical-across-calls system prompts (e.g. layer3_draft.py:67). The plan stage's system prompt (the preamble, ~900 words) is likewise byte-identical across all n_prompts calls.
findings.failure_scenario: No correctness impact; at full scale (5000 plan calls) the identical preamble is re-billed as fresh input tokens on every call. The saving is modest (the preamble may sit near the provider's minimum cacheable size), but the inconsistency also reads as an oversight to the receiving lab reviewing the four stages side by side.
findings.recommendation: Add cache_system=True to the layer12 call for consistency (call_claude/no-op semantics below the cache minimum make it harmless if the preamble is too short to cache), or add a one-line comment stating why it is deliberately omitted.

dimensions.summary: The rebuilt DAD pipeline is in substantially better shape than typical for its churn rate: coverage is 94-100% across the charter files with genuinely behavioral tests (resume-makes-no-calls, fail-open paths, refusal fallbacks are all pinned), extraction is fail-closed everywhere, rejects are checkpointed per-kind (INCOHERENT / draft / refine / scope), and the parallel_map "writes on the main thread" contract is respected in every fan-out. The remaining defects cluster in four places. (1) Truncation/refusal parity is almost — but not quite — complete: 1a and 1b reject stop_reason "refusal" explicitly, while 2b, step 3, and baseline only reject max_tokens/empty/echo, so a mid-stream classifier cut (documented as occurring in this pipeline on welfare topics) can ship a partial draft into the training corpus. (2) The gid registry (git-tracked, shared across runs, consumed by audit_dad/diversity) has three collision/renumbering paths: silent fresh-start on a corrupt file (test-pinned), non-atomic last-writer-wins saves under concurrent runs or git merges, and stamp-before-save crash windows in every stage. (3) The step-1 money path got materially riskier in the rebuild: one pass now holds three paid fan-out stages (1b+1c+1d, ~3x the dealt count in calls) entirely in memory before the first record write, and all retry budgets (draft attempts, gate redraft counts, gate feedback) are process-local, resetting on resume. (4) Structurally, step1_dilemmas.py's 533-line run() with five nested closures and six loop-carried mutable dicts is the file's real comprehension risk — the module's checklist/rendering half is fine and separable. dad_pipeline/run.py, baseline.py, compose_scenarios.py, and reasoning_library.py are clean apart from the noted low-severity items; the offline dealing logic in compose_scenarios is well-validated at deal time before any spend.

findings.title: 2b/step-3/baseline accept refusal-truncated output into records
findings.evidence: step2_responses.py:407 rejects a 2b draft only for `not response or stop_reason == "max_tokens" or looks_like_transcript_echo(...)` — stop_reason "refusal" with non-empty text passes. step3_rewrite.py:91 and baseline.py:64 have the same gap. The API leg returns the raw stop_reason (shared/api.py:735) and 1a documents real mid-stream refusal cuts: "Opus's refusal classifier cutting the stream (seen intermittently on insect-welfare plans, 2026-07-19)" (step1_dilemmas.py:673-679). 1a (step1_dilemmas.py:679) and 1b (step1_dilemmas.py:844) explicitly reject `stop_reason == "refusal"`; api.py:726-729 states the invariant: callers that build training records should reject on stop_reason.
findings.failure_scenario: A 2b response on an insect-welfare dilemma is cut mid-argument by the refusal classifier after several paragraphs (stop_reason="refusal", non-empty text). It passes the line-407 check, is checkpointed into responses.jsonl, and step 3 fluently rewrites the half-finished argument into a plausible-looking training record — silently weaker data on exactly the corpus's core topic, undetectable downstream. A refusal-cut step-3 rewrite ships to final/dad_corpus.jsonl directly.
findings.recommendation: Add `or stop_reason == "refusal"` to the skip conditions at step2_responses.py:407, step3_rewrite.py:91, and baseline.py:64 (skip without checkpointing, same as max_tokens, so --resume retries). For strict parity with 1a, also treat refusal-stopped 2a scope replies as unusable attempts at step2_responses.py:306 instead of parsing them. Add one stub_claude test per stage mirroring test_refusal_stopped_plan_is_retried_with_reason_on_file.

findings.title: gid registry can silently collide or renumber across runs, merges, and crashes
findings.evidence: IdRegistry.__init__ swallows a corrupt registry (`except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError): loaded = {}`, id_registry.py:84-87) and starts every kind back at 1 (assign is `max(table.values(), default=0) + 1`, line 98) — pinned as current behavior by tests/test_id_registry.py:41 (test_corrupt_registry_starts_fresh). save() is a non-atomic full overwrite (lines 105-110) of a git-tracked file shared across runs (`git ls-files` shows outputs/dad/id_registry.json tracked). Every stage stamps gids onto appended records before saving the registry: step1_dilemmas.py:967 (stamp) vs :1003 (save, once per pass); step2_responses.py:469 vs :476; backfill_gids.py rewrites run files incrementally but saves the registry only after ALL runs (line 142-143). Gids are consumed as cross-run join keys by evals/audit_dad.py:167-170 and evals/diversity.py:135-146.
findings.failure_scenario: Two contributors run the pipeline on separate branches; git merge of id_registry.json leaves conflict markers; the next run's IdRegistry silently loads {} and re-mints P-0001/R-0001/E-0001 for new content — numbers already stamped on committed runs for different artifacts. The audit and diversity reports then join different responses under one R-####, misattributing quality evidence across runs. Same collision via crash between record append and registry.save() (unregistered stamped gids get re-allocated to other content by the next run), or via a backfill interrupted before its single end-of-walk save.
findings.recommendation: 1) Fail loudly on an unparseable existing registry (SystemExit telling the user to restore it from git) instead of silently resetting — flip test_corrupt_registry_starts_fresh deliberately. 2) Make save() atomic (write to a temp file in the same dir, os.replace). 3) Save the registry before or atomically with each batch of stamped records (step1 currently saves once per pass; backfill once per invocation — save per run_dir in backfill_run). 4) Document that concurrent DAD runs share one registry and are not safe; consider an fcntl lock or per-run allocation journal if concurrent runs are expected.

Gids are consumed as stable cross-run identifiers by evals/audit_dad.py:167-170 and evals/diversity.py:135-148, and the module's own docstring says gids exist to align artifacts across runs, so collisions misattribute evidence as the scenario describes. | Verified every cited location: silent fresh-start on corrupt registry (id_registry.py:84-91, test-pinned at tests/test_id_registry.py:41), max+1 allocation (line 98), non-atomic overwrite save (105-110), git-tracked shared outputs/dad/id_registry.json with no merge driver, stamp-before-save windows in step1_dilemmas.py (967 vs 1003), step2_responses.py (469 vs 476), and backfill_gids.py's single end-of-walk save (142-143); audit_dad.py:157-170 and diversity.py:135-148 consume gids as cross-run join keys. Severity high is justified for silent cross-run identity corruption of the designed join key, though impact is confined to audit/diversity/viewer attribution, not training-record content.

findings.title: Step-1 pass holds 1b+1c+1d spend in memory; retry budgets reset on resume

dimensions.summary: The DAD corpus-audit subsystem is far stronger than typical eval code: thresholds live in one place (the eval writes display rows + verdicts; the viewer renders them without duplicating logic), the paid pass logs raw unparseable replies to reason_failures.jsonl, extraction failures are counted and rendered as gaps ("a missing bar is a gap, not a zero"), showcase highlights are verbatim-validated fail-closed, and the 88%-covered test suite genuinely exercises failure modes (extraction failure counting, delivery clamps, span rejection). The July SDF failure class ("parse failures counted as clean") was mostly designed out — but not everywhere: three judge-parse slips still silently change metric semantics instead of registering as failures (the corpus-distinct consolidation fallback is the worst, inflating a substance headline with no marker), the per-prompt keying of every response-side section silently drops data on multi-sample runs, and the auto-fired ~370-call paid pass has no checkpointing, so an interruption re-bills everything — against the repo's own money-path rule. The untested 12% is precisely the fallback/skip branches plus main()'s orchestration, and the 0%-coverage viewer page still computes a few headline percent claims inline (most decision logic correctly lives in tested rendering.py). Structurally, the 2,997-line module is navigable via consistent section banners and data-driven YAML maps, but it has visibly outgrown one file (duplicate section banners, a "main" divider 480 lines before main, a 185-statement audit_reasons); it needs a mechanical package split before delivery, not a rewrite.

findings.title: Viewer audit page computes headline percent claims inline, duplicating the same lift with two definitions, at 0% coverage
findings.evidence: The page mostly honors the repo's Streamlit-stays-logic-free rule (row-building lives in tested viewer/rendering.py), but the boldfaced numeric claims a lab reads first are computed inline in the 1,337-line, 0%-covered page: _render_pareto (317-319) derives '+X% considerations' from mpr.mean_unique while the headline block (380-384) derives its 'adds X% more' from _ic.parent (mean_reasoning+mean_alternative, with a different legacy-report reconstruction path at audit_dad.py:2842-2849) — two computations of the same claim that diverge on legacy-shaped reports; line 317 also guards b_mean but not bm before dividing by it. Additional in-page logic: Pearson-r computation (866-867), gloss-parsing fallback (1104-1107), and Pareto mean-diamonds recomputed from the both-axes-filtered subset (351) rather than the report's recorded means.
findings.failure_scenario: A refactor of the report shape (like the recent reasons/alternatives merge) changes one lift computation but not the other; the page then shows '+42% considerations' in the Pareto blurb and 'adds 55% more' in the headline for the same run — contradictory quality evidence in the artifact shown to the receiving lab — and no test can catch it because the file has zero coverage.
findings.recommendation: Move the lift/tradeoff computations into viewer/rendering.py as pure functions (e.g., audit_headline_lifts(report) returning one consistent pair used by both blocks), add tests covering current + legacy report shapes and the plain-mean-zero edge, and have the page only format the returned values — matching the pattern already used for every chart-row helper.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified all cited lines in viewer/ui_pages/audit.py (1,337 lines, no test references ui_pages): lines 315-319 compute the Pareto blurb lift inline from moral_patient_reasons.mean_unique, and the guard `None not in (pm, bm, p_mean, b_mean) and b_mean` checks b_mean's truthiness but only bm's None-ness before dividing `pm / bm` at line 319. Lines 380-384 compute the headline lift from _ic["parent"], which evals/audit_dad.py builds as mean_reasoning + mean_alternative (2838-2841) with the legacy reconstruction path exactly at 2842-2849 (reasons = old mean_unique, alternatives = old moves block) — so the two lifts measure the same claim via different paths and genuinely diverge on legacy-shaped reports where mean_unique excludes alternatives. The secondary instances also hold: inline Pearson r at 866-867, gloss-parsing fallback at 1104-1107, and line 351's mean diamonds recomputed via df.groupby over rows that rendering.audit_delivery_pareto_rows explicitly filters to records with both axes, rather than the report's recorded pipeline_mean/plain_mean.

findings.title: Response-openings gloss claims a pipeline-vs-plain comparison the check never performs
findings.evidence: The section gloss stored in the report and rendered verbatim by the viewer says 'WHAT: which opening MOVE each reply uses, pipeline vs plain Claude — named families are known tics', but audit_response_openings only reads pipeline drafts (step2/responses.jsonl) and finals; openings_dad.load_responses (openings_dad.py:104-122) has no baseline-arm path, and no plain-arm numbers appear in any row of the section.
findings.failure_scenario: A lab reviewer reading the audit page's methodology text believes opener-family collapse was measured against the plain-Claude control (as every neighboring response section genuinely is) and treats the family shares as a differential signal; the stated methodology of the delivered quality evidence is wrong.
findings.recommendation: Either scan _baseline_by_prompt_id through the same stage_stats and add a plain column (consistent with the sibling sections), or correct the gloss to say the check covers pipeline drafts and finals only.

findings.title: Jargon pipeline-vs-plain excess computed over un-intersected arm populations
findings.evidence: `excess = total - sum(b_counts.values())` with the inline comment '(same prompts)', but pipe comes from the step3/final join and plain from baseline_responses.jsonl with no key intersection; the verdict divides max(excess,0) by n=len(pipe). audit_response_lengths (741-748) and rendering.audit_batch_totals both deliberately restrict to paired records — this section doesn't.

findings.recommendation: Intersect the two dicts on prompt_id before totalling (pipe_paired = {k: v for k, v in pipe.items() if k in plain}), report the paired n in the row, and add a test with asymmetric arm coverage.

findings.title: Curated YAML data files: syntax/regex errors crash the whole audit; review_tics writes raw text and can't filter the plain arm
findings.evidence: load_moves compiles moves.yaml patterns with re.compile and catches only FileNotFoundError (918-921); load_tic_lists/load_tic_surfaces likewise catch only FileNotFoundError (774-777, 794-797) — a YAML syntax error or invalid regex introduced by the promote/curation workflow raises uncaught, killing the entire audit (including the free sections and the auto post-run eval subprocess). review_tics.py builds YAML by raw string insertion (promote line 99 quotes the phrase but not `family`; ignore_phrase line 118 same for reason), so a value containing a double quote or colon corrupts tics.yaml and triggers exactly that crash on the next run. Its `list --arm` choices (line 168) omit 'plain' even though the audit's mirror screen writes plain-arm candidates (audit_dad.py:2762) and the viewer displays them.

findings.recommendation: Catch yaml.YAMLError and re.error in the three loaders and degrade to an explicit skipped-section row naming the bad file/pattern; in review_tics, yaml-escape inserted values (yaml.safe_dump the inline map) and validate the file round-trips with yaml.safe_load before writing; add 'plain' to the --arm choices.

findings.title: Carried-forward paid data has no staleness marker in the report JSON or viewer
findings.evidence: carry_forward_reasons copies moral_patient_reasons/delivery/showcase/reason_composition from the previous report wholesale; the only indication is a terminal print in main() (2977-2978). The JSON carries no carried_forward flag or original-pass timestamp, so the viewer renders the paid headline, Pareto scatter, and showcase identically whether the numbers were measured against the current corpus or a previous state of it.
findings.failure_scenario: A run is resumed and step 3 produces additional final records; a free offline audit re-run refreshes all offline sections against the new corpus but carries the paid sections from the smaller corpus; the viewer shows a considerations headline and showcase whose underlying response set no longer matches the offline sections beside them, with no visible indicator.
findings.recommendation: Stamp report['moral_patient_reasons']['carried_forward'] = {'from_n': old n, 'at': old report timestamp} in carry_forward_reasons, warn when the carried per_case keys differ from the current _final_by_prompt_id keys, and render a small caption in the viewer when the flag is present.

dimensions.summary: The HF publishing path is one of the strongest-engineered modules in the repo, and the code matches CLAUDE.md's documented contract on every headline claim I checked: delete_patterns are correctly scoped to the published pipeline (evals/publish_hf.py:682-683, asserted by tests/test_publish_hf.py:710-722); the rmtree guard from PR history (397552e/bfa1bc4) exists and covers staging-dir == run_dir, run_dir/final, and run_dir/audit with four regression tests; report_content.json (the only editorial input) is verifiably excluded from staging and upload; the sibling's metadata is fetched outside the staging tree so neither its files nor hf_hub_download's .cache dir can enter the upload (asserted at test line 899-909); --dry-run provably makes zero Hub calls (raise_on_call stub); and the card is built from measured audit fields with per-stage model overrides surfaced, exactly as documented. Token handling is clean: HF_TOKEN is loaded via load_dotenv and picked up by huggingface_hub's own env handling — it is never printed, staged, or written to any manifest or card, and the card's Source link matches the actual git remote (sentfutures org). The ruff PLW1510 subprocess finding is in dad_pipeline/run.py:61, not in this file — nothing subprocess-related exists in the publishing path. The untested 3% is precisely the three unwrapped Hub seams (_create_repo, _list_repo_files, _download_file bodies) plus the __main__ guard. The residual risks are at the edges the tests could not reach: stage_run will still rmtree any pre-existing directory that isn't the input run (a wrong --staging-dir can delete a different paid run wholesale, in --dry-run too); a re-publish reusing an existing --tag silently leaves the tag on the old commit while printing success (a stale version pointer on a public dataset); and the whole delete-then-add correctness rests on huggingface_hub's add-wins-over-delete precedence under a floor-only version pin (>=0.25). These are all small, targeted fixes; none undermine the overall assessment that this delivery mechanism is careful, well-documented, and unusually well-tested.

findings.title: stage_run rmtree deletes any pre-existing --staging-dir that isn't the input run — including other paid run directories
findings.evidence: stage_run wipes the staging target unconditionally: `if staging_dir.exists(): shutil.rmtree(staging_dir)` (lines 145-146). The guard above (lines 129-139) only refuses a staging dir that equals/contains THIS run_dir, run_dir/final, or run_dir/audit. Any other existing directory — a sibling run under outputs/sdf/runs/, or any user directory — passes the guard and is recursively deleted. The guard's own comment acknowledges mistyped --staging-dir as the threat model ("an easy typo, since those are real, well-known subdirectory names"), and tests (test_publish_hf.py:218-249) only cover the three self-overlap cases. Note --dry-run runs the same stage_run wipe, so the "no Hub API calls" safety promise does not extend to local disk.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator publishes run A and tab-completes the wrong path into --staging-dir: `python evals/publish_hf.py --input outputs/sdf/runs/2026-07-25_run-A --staging-dir outputs/sdf/runs/2026-07-20_local_full-scale`. The guard passes (run B is not run A), rmtree silently deletes run B — an uncommitted local_* full-scale run worth $50-500 of paid API calls — before any output appears. The same happens under --dry-run, which the user reasonably believes is side-effect-free.
findings.recommendation: Before rmtree, refuse any pre-existing non-empty --staging-dir that wasn't created by this tool: have stage_run drop a marker file (e.g. .publish_hf_staging) into every staging root it creates, and only rmtree a non-empty existing dir if the marker is present (or if its entries are limited to README.md/sdf/dad). Add regression tests mirroring test_staging_dir_equal_to_run_dir_is_rejected for a sibling run dir and an arbitrary populated dir.
instances: evals/publish_hf.py:129-139 (guard limited to the input run's own paths)
findings.verifier_notes: Verified evals/publish_hf.py at current main: the unconditional `shutil.rmtree(staging_dir)` is at lines 145-146, and the guard at lines 129-139 only rejects staging dirs that equal/contain run_dir, run_dir/final, or run_dir/audit — any other existing directory (including a sibling paid run) passes and is recursively deleted. The --dry-run claim holds: main() calls stage_run (line 604) before the dry-run branch (line 629), so a user-supplied --staging-dir is wiped even in dry-run mode despite the "no Hub API calls made" message. Tests at tests/test_publish_hf.py:218-249 cover only the three self-overlap rejection cases plus the containing-run_dir case; no test protects sibling directories, and the wipe-on-reuse behavior is asserted as intentional at lines 199-216. | Verified evals/publish_hf.py lines 129-146: the guard only refuses staging dirs that equal/contain run_dir, run_dir/final, or run_dir/audit, then rmtree unconditionally deletes any other pre-existing --staging-dir with no prompt. main() calls stage_run (line 604) before the --dry-run early return (line 629), so --dry-run with --staging-dir performs the same wipe (dry-run without --staging-dir uses a fresh mkdtemp and is safe — consistent with the scenario as stated). tests/test_publish_hf.py:218-249 covers only the self-overlap rejections plus a nested-allowed case; no test protects a sibling run directory. Severity high is justified: uncommitted local_* full-scale runs are gitignored siblings under outputs/*/runs/, exactly the tab-completion-adjacent targets, and the guard's own comment names mistyped paths as the threat model.

findings.title: Re-publish with an existing --tag silently leaves the tag on the old commit while printing success
findings.evidence: _create_tag passes exist_ok=True (line 558) so "a retried publish with the same --tag (e.g. after fixing a typo'd --input) must not die here". I verified installed huggingface_hub 1.25.1: create_tag with exist_ok=True swallows the 409 and does NOT move the existing tag. main() then prints `Tag: {args.tag}` (line 690) unconditionally. The comment's own motivating scenario — first publish completed with a typo'd --input, then re-published corrected with the same tag — is exactly the case where the tag was already created on the bad commit and now silently stays there.
findings.failure_scenario: Publish run A with --tag sdf-v1-fullscale (tag lands on commit A, wrong data). Fix --input, republish with the same tag: the corrected corpus uploads as commit B, create_tag 409s and is swallowed, the script prints "Tag: sdf-v1-fullscale" as if applied. Anyone loading the dataset with revision="sdf-v1-fullscale" — e.g. the frontier lab pinning the delivered snapshot — gets the typo'd run's data forever, with the script's own output claiming otherwise.
findings.recommendation: In _create_tag, catch the exists case explicitly (or pre-check via list_repo_refs): if the tag already exists, compare its target commit to the just-created upload commit; if they differ, print a loud warning telling the operator to delete_tag and re-tag (or offer a --retag flag that does delete_tag + create_tag). Never print "Tag: X" when the tag was not actually moved to this commit.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified evals/publish_hf.py at current checkout: line 558 passes exist_ok=True in _create_tag, and main() prints "Tag: {args.tag}" at line 690 whenever --tag is given, with no existence check or tag move. Verified installed huggingface_hub 1.25.1 source (hf_api.py:7120-7125): create_tag swallows a 409 when exist_ok=True and never relocates an existing tag, and _create_tag passes no revision anyway. So a same-tag republish after a bad first publish leaves the tag on the old commit while the script reports success — exactly the finding's failure scenario. Cited lines and both claimed instances (553-558, 685-690) are accurate.

findings.title: Publish correctness depends on upload_folder's add-wins-over-delete precedence under a floor-only huggingface_hub pin
findings.evidence: delete_patterns [f"{pipeline_tag}/audit/*", f"{pipeline_tag}/card_meta.json"] (lines 682-683) match the very files being freshly staged in the same commit — every publish uploads sdf/audit/*.json while also listing sdf/audit/* for deletion. The comment (lines 679-681) says this is "Safe... because upload_folder drops any deletion whose path is also being added", "verified against the installed huggingface_hub" — but requirements.txt:14 pins only `huggingface_hub>=0.25` (installed: 1.25.1; the floor spans a full major-version range), and no test or runtime check can verify the real library's precedence (stub_hf replaces the wrapper entirely).
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor or CI environment resolves a huggingface_hub version whose delete/add precedence differs (or a future release changes it): every publish then uploads and immediately deletes its own audit files and card_meta.json, publishing the corpus with the quality-evidence directory silently missing from the public dataset — exactly the misstated-evidence failure the card exists to prevent.
findings.recommendation: Pin a tested version range for huggingface_hub in requirements.txt (e.g. >=1.0,<2), and add a cheap post-publish verification in main(): call _list_repo_files after upload and assert every staged path (relative to staging_dir) is present, failing loudly if any staged file is missing from the commit.

findings.title: Card lists per-stage model overrides as a nameless de-duplicated set, losing which stage each model ran
findings.evidence: models_used collects `sorted({v for k, v in ... if k.endswith("_model") ...})` (lines 304-307) — the knob names (k) are discarded and values de-duplicated — and _dataset_section renders "- **per-stage models**: `m1`, `m2`" (lines 337-338). CLAUDE.md's rationale for this feature is provenance accuracy ("the per-stage *_model knobs... are what actually generated the records"), but the rendered card cannot distinguish a model that did the alignment-critical layer-4 rewrite from one that only did layer-5 scoring.
findings.failure_scenario: A run with sdf.draft_model=claude-haiku-4-5 and sdf.score_model=claude-opus-5 (Opus only judging, never generating) renders "per-stage models: claude-haiku-4-5, claude-opus-5" — a lab reader reasonably concludes Opus generated content when it only scored it; the converse misreading (assuming the cheap model wrote the corpus) is equally available. The provenance claim the card was built to make is ambiguous exactly where it matters.
findings.recommendation: Render knob->model pairs instead of a value set: change models_used to return sorted (knob, model) tuples for overrides differing from the default, and render e.g. "- **per-stage models**: `rewrite_model: claude-opus-5`, `score_model: claude-opus-5`". Update test_card_surfaces_per_stage_model_overrides and TestModelsUsed accordingly.

findings.title: DAD language metadata hardcoded to ["en"], ignoring the run's language_distribution in the staged manifest
findings.evidence: detected_languages returns ["en"] for any non-sdf pipeline (lines 275-276). The docstring justifies this by the dad language_distribution DEFAULT being English-only, but config.yaml:95 shows language_distribution is a real knob (currently `en: 1.0`), and the run's full config snapshot — including that knob — is already staged in run_manifest.json right next to where detected_languages reads audit_report.json. The measured/declared truth is available and unread.
findings.failure_scenario: A future DAD run sets language_distribution to e.g. {en: 0.5, es: 0.5}; publishing it declares language: [en] in the card frontmatter. Hub language filtering, the dataset viewer, and anyone relying on the card's metadata misdescribe a half-Spanish corpus as English-only — on a card whose stated design is 'built entirely from measured fields'.
findings.recommendation: In detected_languages, for the dad pipeline read the staged run_manifest.json's config.language_distribution (keys with weight > 0, mapped through the existing LANGUAGE_CODES-style codes — dad's keys are already ISO codes) and fall back to ["en"] only when absent. Add a test with a multilingual language_distribution manifest.

findings.title: Untested 3% is the three Hub-API wrapper bodies whose hardcoded kwargs are safety-relevant
findings.evidence: Coverage misses lines 427-428 (_create_repo body), 447-448 (_list_repo_files), 452-453 (_download_file), and 694 (__main__ guard). The stub_hf fixture (tests/conftest.py:249-309) replaces all five wrappers at the module boundary, so end-to-end tests never execute these bodies; TestHubApiWrappers (test_publish_hf.py:596-635) gives _upload_folder and _create_tag direct fake-HfApi tests asserting their kwargs (exist_ok=True, delete_patterns forwarding), but the other three wrappers have no such tests — their repo_type="dataset", exist_ok=True, and local_dir kwargs are never asserted anywhere.

dimensions.summary: The shared infrastructure has grown substantially since July and is in good shape overall. (a) Backend parity: the bedrock leg reuses the api code path (same retry classification via anthropic exception types, max_tokens enforced, model ids translated only at the wire, unsupported models fail loudly) and is test-covered; pricing constants in _PRICING were verified against current published rates (Opus 5 $5/$25, Fable $10/$50, Haiku $1/$5) and the prompt-cache multipliers (1.25x write / 0.1x read) are correct, as is the temperature-rejection gate for the Claude 5 family / Opus 4.7+. (b) The auto backend's empty-system api-leg rule is correctly implemented (`use_cc = _cc_demoted is None and bool(full_system)`), demotion is loud, sticky, re-serves the failed call, never triggers on per-item refusals, and every cost record names the effective backend — all pinned by tests. (c) Thread-safety under parallel_map is handled: cost-log appends are lock-serialized, attempt counters are thread-local, and the remaining warn-flag/demotion races are benign duplicates. (e) July's positive claims still hold: parallel_map keeps its in-order, main-thread-writes contract, and cost logs are per-run (each run.py passes run_dir/cost_log.jsonl) with stage/item_id/backend tags. (f) The vendored 1.68MB cl100k_base blob is keyed by tiktoken's own sha1 cache name, wired via TIKTOKEN_CACHE_DIR setdefault, and the offline-tests guarantee holds (token-boundary tests run under pytest-socket in the required smoke check). The real residual risks are at the seams: the subscription path deliberately doesn't enforce max_tokens, and the DAD/pref truncation gates are fail-open equality checks that only work on the api backend's stop_reason vocabulary (SDF's gates are fail-closed and correct); the Gemini embeddings leg trusts response alignment with no length check while the embedding cache makes any misalignment permanent; and token-level truncation of embedding inputs is silent, so a diversity report can understate how much text its metrics actually saw.

findings.title: DAD/pref truncation gates fail open on subscription-served (claude_code/auto) calls
findings.evidence: call_claude's docstring states max_tokens is "Enforced on the api backend only — Claude Code applies its own output cap"; the claude_code leg returns whatever stop_reason the CLI's ResultMessage carries (claude_agent_sdk types.py declares `stop_reason: str | None = None`) and api.py:677 only WARNS on non-end_turn values. The DAD and pref gates test equality with one value: dad_pipeline/baseline.py:64 `if not response or stop_reason == "max_tokens"`, dad_pipeline/step2_responses.py:407, dad_pipeline/step3_rewrite.py:91, pref_pipeline/run.py:166, dad_pipeline/step1_dilemmas.py:371/688. By contrast every SDF layer gates fail-closed: sdf_pipeline/layer3_draft.py:84 `if stop != "end_turn"`.
findings.failure_scenario: A dev run on backend claude_code (the documented default for dev runs) has a response truncated by the CLI's own output cap, and the CLI reports stop_reason as None or a value other than 'max_tokens' (the field is Optional and CLI-version-dependent). The truncated text is not caught by `stop_reason == "max_tokens"`, passes the non-empty check, is checkpointed as a completed DAD training record, and --resume never retries it — a mid-sentence assistant reply lands in dad_corpus.jsonl with only a stderr warning scrolled past. The same records survive step 3 because its gate has the same shape.
findings.recommendation: Normalize the gate to fail-closed like the SDF layers: in each DAD/pref call site replace `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` rejection with acceptance-only-on `stop_reason in ("end_turn", "stop_sequence")` (refusal is already surfaced as 'refusal' and empty text). Alternatively, normalize inside call_claude: map any claude_code stop_reason outside the known api vocabulary to a sentinel the callers already reject. Add one test driving a DAD step through stub_claude returning stop_reason=None to pin the behavior.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified every cited line: api.py:583-586 docstring matches the quote, api.py:543 returns the SDK ResultMessage stop_reason unchanged (declared `str | None = None` in claude_agent_sdk/types.py:1034/1209), and api.py:677 only warns on non-end_turn/stop_sequence values before returning the text. All seven DAD/pref gates test `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` exactly as cited, while SDF layers (layer12_plan.py:84, layer3_draft.py:84, layer4_rewrite.py:76) gate `stop != "end_turn"` fail-closed; step2_responses.py:407 and step3_rewrite.py:91 accept free prose with no structural check, and checkpoint.mark_done (step3_rewrite.py:123) makes the truncated record permanent under --resume, so the scenario holds. Minor nuances that don't overturn it: step1_dilemmas' gates (371, 679/688) are backed by closed-tag parsing that usually catches truncation, and step2's scope gate (306) is followed by _valid_scope — the unmitigated path is exactly step2 drafts, step3 rewrites, baseline, and pref arms.

findings.title: Gemini embeddings leg never validates vector count/order against the batch
findings.evidence: `vectors = [e["values"] for e in resp.json()["embeddings"]]` returns whatever the batchEmbedContents response contains, with no check that len(vectors) == len(batch) and no per-item index to order by. The OpenAI leg is defensive (_openai_normalize sorts by d.index, embeddings.py:206-209, and has a test pinning it); the Gemini leg has nothing. Downstream, evals/diversity.py embed_with_cache (diversity.py:209-215) zips the returned vectors against the requested texts and persists them into embeddings_cache.npz keyed by sha256(model+text).
findings.failure_scenario: A Gemini response omits or reorders entries (partial failure, API contract change, or an error object in the embeddings array). zip() in embed_with_cache silently pairs vector k with text k anyway, every document after the gap gets its neighbor's embedding, and the misattributed vectors are written to the per-run embedding cache — so the delivered diversity_report.json names the wrong documents as near-duplicates, and reruns reuse the poisoned cache instead of correcting it.
findings.recommendation: In _gemini_transport, after parsing, raise (e.g. GeminiTransientError for a retry, or ValueError to fail loudly) when len(vectors) != len(batch) or when any entry lacks 'values'. Mirror the OpenAI-leg test with a stubbed short response asserting the loud failure.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified shared/embeddings.py:201 is exactly `vectors = [e["values"] for e in resp.json()["embeddings"]]` with no len(vectors)==len(batch) check, and Gemini batchEmbedContents entries carry no index; embed_texts just `rows.extend(vectors)` with no count check either. The OpenAI leg does sort by d.index (_openai_normalize, lines 206-209) and tests/test_embeddings.py:112 pins that ordering. Downstream, evals/diversity.py embed_with_cache (lines 209-215) zips idxs with vectors — zip truncates silently, so a gap shifts every later vector onto its neighbor's text — and persists misattributed vectors to audit/embeddings_cache.npz (keyed sha256(model+text), saved after every chunk before any consistency check), so reruns reuse the poisoned cache. Minor nuance not affecting the verdict: a pure omission would also leave the final missing key unpopulated, crashing np.stack (KeyError, diversity.py:218) on the first run — but the poisoned cache is already saved and the rerun then delivers the wrong report; a pure reorder is fully silent as claimed.

findings.title: Token-level truncation of embedding inputs is silent and uncounted in the diversity report
findings.evidence: embed_texts silently truncates every input to the model token window: `texts = [truncate_to_tokens(t, cap, model) for t in texts]` (cap = 8192 OpenAI / 2048 Gemini). The only caller, evals/diversity.py, counts truncation solely at the character level: `truncated = sum(1 for _, text, _ in sampled if len(text) > args.max_chars)` (diversity.py:552) and reports it as n_truncated (diversity.py:584-585). The boundary itself is correct and test-pinned (tests/test_embeddings.py TestTokenTruncation, offline via the vendored cl100k ranks), but no count of token-capped texts ever reaches the report. The docstring even acknowledges: "Callers that care about how much was cut should truncate (and report) first" — the caller doesn't.
findings.failure_scenario: A matrix-pipeline SDF run with native-script documents (the matrix cultures include Japan/China written in their languages — shared/entity_pools.py:101-122): a 7,000-char Japanese document is ~8.7k cl100k tokens, over the 8192 OpenAI window, and far over Gemini's 2048. Every such document is embedded as a prefix; n_truncated reports 0 because 7000 chars <= max_chars; the delivered diversity_report.json presents near-dup rates and Vendi scores computed on fractional documents with no disclosure. On a Gemini run (GEMINI_API_KEY only), even a typical ~4k-token English SDF doc is halved silently once max_chars is raised.
findings.recommendation: Make the truncation observable: either have embed_texts return/expose a count of token-capped inputs (or accept a callback), or have diversity.py pre-truncate with truncate_to_tokens and count how many texts changed, reporting a token_truncated row next to the char-level one. Add a warning when the resolved model is gemini-* and typical corpus documents exceed 2048 tokens.
findings.corrected_claim: embed_texts silently truncates every input to the model token window at shared/embeddings.py:300 (cap = 8192 OpenAI / 2048 Gemini), and its docstring (lines 285-286) explicitly delegates reporting to callers. Its two callers are evals/diversity.py and evals/openings_dad.py:194 (embedding_report, which embeds first sentences too short for the cap to matter); the material caller, diversity.py, counts truncation solely at the character level (line 552, default --max-chars 7000) and reports it as "truncated for embedding" (lines 583-585) and n_truncated (line 752), so no count of token-capped texts ever reaches the report. Consequence as stated: a matrix-pipeline native-script (e.g. Japanese, ~1.25-1.5 cl100k tokens/char) document of 7,000 chars exceeds the 8192-token OpenAI window and is embedded as a prefix while n_truncated reports 0; on a GEMINI_API_KEY-only run (2048-token cap) the silent cut becomes severe once max_chars is raised.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified shared/embeddings.py:300 (silent token truncation, caps 8192/2048 at lines 58/76), the verbatim docstring at lines 285-286, diversity.py:552 char-only counting with default max_chars=7000, the CJK token math (backed by the code's own comments at embeddings.py:50-51 and diversity.py:525-527), native-script matrix cultures in entity_pools.py:96-121, the GEMINI_API_KEY-only default-model path (embeddings.py:104-107), and TestTokenTruncation at tests/test_embeddings.py:155. Two details are wrong: diversity.py is not the only caller of embed_texts (evals/openings_dad.py:194 also calls it, on first sentences where the cap is immaterial), and the n_truncated JSON key is at diversity.py:752 — lines 584-585 are the printed/report-section "truncated for embedding" entries. Core claim and failure scenario hold as stated.

dimensions.summary: Delivery-readiness has improved substantially in substance but the process/tooling posture is unchanged since July, and a handful of doc/hygiene items would be the first things a receiving lab trips over. The good news first: CLAUDE.md is unusually well-maintained against the rebuilt architecture — I verified the auto-evals claim (config.yaml dad.evals.auto wired through dad_pipeline/run.py:35-68), the publish_hf delete_patterns scoping (publish_hf.py:682), the matrix config keys (config.yaml:30-32), INCOHERENT checkpointing (layer12_plan.py), and .env.example's existence; .gitattributes deliberately handles both committed runs and the vendored blob; and a scan of all 998 committed output files found no API keys, HF tokens, or emails. The bad news: (1) the toolchain gap is now bigger in absolute terms — 16.8k source LOC across 48 files with a 7-line pyproject.toml, no lockfile, no lint/format/type/coverage gate, CI still compileall+pytest, and today's mechanical run shows 140 ruff errors, 157 mypy errors, 64/71 files unformatted, 68% coverage with several shipping modules at 0%; (2) requirements drift is real (numpy imported in four source modules but undeclared; tqdm/jsonlines dead; seven deps fully unpinned) meaning the exact environment that generated the delivered corpora is unreproducible; (3) committed audit reports leak a contributor's macOS home path, and publish_hf.py uploads those same files verbatim to the public HF dataset; (4) CLAUDE.md's dad_segmented/ reference points at a directory that has never existed in git history — a trust-damaging error in the one file agents and lab engineers read first; (5) the README's setup clone URL still points at the pre-rename GitHub org (org renames don't redirect and the old name is squattable); and (6) open issue #53 asserts "SDF is currently broken out-of-the-box on main" against code that no longer exists. All but the tooling program are under-a-day fixes; I'd treat the path-leak scrub, the dad_segmented reconciliation, the org-URL fix, and closing #53 as pre-delivery blockers on effort-to-impact grounds.

findings.title: Requirements drift: numpy imported but undeclared, tqdm/jsonlines dead, seven deps unpinned, no lockfile
findings.evidence: numpy is imported directly in shared/textstats.py:21, shared/embeddings.py:31, evals/audit_dad.py:41, evals/diversity.py:59 (and tests/conftest.py:36) but does not appear in requirements.txt — it installs only as a transitive dependency of pandas/streamlit. shared/__init__.py's Python-floor comment even says 'matching numpy' for a dep the file never declares. tqdm (line 6) and jsonlines (line 7) are imported nowhere in the repo (verified by grep). pandas, pyyaml, python-dotenv, tqdm, jsonlines, tenacity, faker carry no version constraint at all; the rest are floors-only; there is no lockfile of any kind in the repo root.
findings.failure_scenario: A future pandas release that relaxes its numpy requirement, or a contributor slimming deps, silently breaks four modules including the diversity eval. More important for delivery: the exact dependency set that generated the shipped corpora is unreproducible — a lab re-running an audit with a different numpy/pandas/wordfreq resolution can get different near-dup/diversity numbers than the committed reports, with no way to tell whether the pipeline or the environment changed.
findings.recommendation: Add `numpy>=1.26` explicitly; delete tqdm and jsonlines; generate and commit a lock (uv `uv pip compile` or pip-tools `requirements.lock.txt`) from the floors file, and switch ci.yml to install from the lock so CI proves the pinned set. Record the lock hash in run_manifest.json if you want run-level reproducibility.
findings.verifier_notes: All factual assertions verified against current main. numpy is imported at exactly the cited lines (shared/textstats.py:21, shared/embeddings.py:31, evals/audit_dad.py:41, evals/diversity.py:59, tests/conftest.py:36) and appears nowhere in requirements.txt, while shared/__init__.py:3 justifies MIN_PYTHON with "numpy needs >=3.12". grep finds zero imports of tqdm or jsonlines anywhere in the repo, yet they sit at requirements.txt:6-7; pandas, pyyaml, python-dotenv, tqdm, jsonlines, tenacity, faker (lines 3-8, 10) carry no version constraint, all others are floors-only, and no lockfile exists in the repo root (pyproject.toml contains only pytest config, no dependency section). The failure/reproducibility scenario follows directly from numpy being purely transitive and the dependency set being unresolvable to a fixed state.

findings.title: Committed audit reports embed a contributor's home path; publish_hf.py uploads those files verbatim to the public HF dataset
findings.evidence: audit_dad.py:2919, diversity.py:745, and audit_sdf.py:561 all write `"input": str(args.input)` into their reports. Three committed files already carry `/Users/<contributor>/Documents/alignment-data-pipeline/...` (a contributor's macOS username and home layout), public on GitHub now: outputs/dad/runs/2026-07-19_18-11_smoke3-postmerge/audit/audit_report.json and diversity_report.json, and outputs/dad/runs/2026-07-20_20-51_bedrock-40/audit/diversity_report.json. evals/publish_hf.py:173-178 stages every audit/*.{json,jsonl,html} file verbatim (excluding only report_content.json), so publishing any such run puts the path on the public Hugging Face dataset. bedrock-40 is the newest committed DAD run — if it was the run behind the just-merged DAD config publish (PRs #105/#106), the path is already live on sentientfutures/animal-welfare-mid-training-datasets.
findings.failure_scenario: Any contributor who runs an audit (or whose auto-eval resolves an absolute run path) bakes their machine username into a report that the repo's conventions then commit and publish. The lab receiving the repo — and anyone browsing the public HF dataset — sees contributors' local usernames and directory structures; scrubbing after publication requires a force-push/re-upload and the git history keeps it forever.
findings.recommendation: Change all three writers to record a repo-relative or run-id-only value (`Path(args.input).name` or relpath against PIPELINE_OUTPUT_ROOT); add a belt-and-braces sanitizer in publish_hf.py stage_run that rewrites any `/Users/<contributor>` or `/home/<contributor>` prefix in staged JSON `input` fields; scrub the three committed files in a small PR; and check whether the published DAD config on the Hub carries the path — if so re-publish after the scrub.

findings.title: README setup instructions still point at the pre-rename GitHub org (Mycelium-tools)
findings.evidence: README.md:121: `git clone https://github.com/Mycelium-tools/alignment-data-pipeline.git`; git-workflow-guide.md:57 gives a PR-creation URL under the same old org. findings.failure_scenario: A lab engineer following the README's own setup section clones a URL that 404s today — or, if the abandoned org name is ever registered by a third party, clones someone else's repository, which is a textbook namesquatting supply-chain vector for a repo about to be handed to a frontier lab.
findings.recommendation: Update both URLs to the sentfutures org (or make them org-agnostic: 'clone your fork / this repo's URL'); grep the repo for 'Mycelium' before delivery and consider registering or archiving awareness of the old org name.

The stale URLs should still be updated — the transfer redirect is fragile (it silently breaks if a same-named repo is ever created under the old org) — but the "404s today / namesquattable vacated org" scenario is wrong, and severity should be low rather than medium.

findings.title: Vendored 1.68MB tiktoken BPE blob has no in-tree provenance, license, or refresh note
findings.evidence: vendor/tiktoken/ contains a single 1,681,126-byte file named only by its cache hash (the cl100k_base BPE ranks). The rationale lives solely in shared/embeddings.py:60-67 (offline tests + fresh CI can't fetch the ranks). .gitattributes:10 correctly marks the path binary/linguist-vendored, but the vendor directory itself carries no README, no license attribution (the ranks ship from openai/tiktoken, MIT), no source URL, and no instructions for regenerating the file if the embedding model or encoding changes.
findings.failure_scenario: Concrete maintenance/delivery cost: a lab's third-party-code audit finds an opaque hash-named 1.6MB blob with no license or provenance and has to reverse-engineer it from a comment in a different module; a future contributor switching embedding models won't know how to produce the sibling cache file (the filename is the sha1 of tiktoken's download URL, which is nowhere written down).
findings.recommendation: Add vendor/tiktoken/README.md stating: what the file is (cl100k_base ranks), where it came from (openai/tiktoken's public blob URL), its license (MIT, with a copy of or pointer to the upstream LICENSE), why it's vendored (embeddings.py:60-67 rationale), and the one-liner to regenerate it (run tiktoken with TIKTOKEN_CACHE_DIR=vendor/tiktoken and copy the resulting cache file).
